title: All woven together
hookLine: think of the universe as one living being, all things woven (Meditations 4.40)

lines: MORE HANDS THAN YOU CAN COUNT.
cards: Pick up the nearest cup. Somebody dug the clay or melted the sand. Somebody fired it in a kiln; somebody else built the kiln.
A truck driver carried it on a road a crew paved, in a truck built in a factory somewhere you've never been. Now the coffee inside: a farmer on a hillside, a picker, a roaster, a ship's crew.
You're holding more people's work than you could count, in one hand, and you'll never meet most of them. The Stoics had a word for that feeling of everything touching everything. Today: sympatheia.

teach.b: Sympatheia is Greek: sym, together, plus pathos, feeling or being affected. Being affected together.

It's the root of our word sympathy, but the Stoics meant something bigger than feeling sorry for someone: every part of the world is connected to every other, so what happens in one place is felt in another.

One example they reached for was the moon and the sea. The Stoic Posidonius, a scientist as well as a philosopher, studied how the tides rise and fall with the moon, and saw in it a sign of one connected cosmos.
Marcus Aurelius made it a daily exercise.
In George Long's 1862 translation, he tells himself: "Constantly regard the universe as one living being, having one substance and one soul."

He pictures all things working together as causes of one another, like threads spun into a single web. Elsewhere he writes that all things are bound up with each other, and in that way friendly to each other.
Why did this matter to an emperor?

teach.h: NO ONE IS TRULY A STRANGER.
teach.b: On this view, if everything is woven together, no one is truly a stranger, and no act is truly private. How you treat the person who made your cup, even without meeting them, is part of the same fabric.

A warning, honestly given: the Stoics also used sympatheia to defend astrology and divination, and ancient critics, Cicero among them, pushed back hard. The idea comes as a package, and readers sort it differently.
The plainest part of it is the cup in your hand: it carries the work of people you'll never meet.

how: Stoic practitioners use Marcus Aurelius's exercise of picturing the universe as one living whole, and reflect on the many people whose work sustains their day.

o: feeling sorry for someone who is having a hard time
a gift sent to a family that is grieving
the idea that all things are connected and affect each other

s: for the Stoics, sympatheia meant pity
it meant the whole cosmos is connected, each part affected by the others.
Posidonius linked the tides to the moon
he saw it as a sign of one connected world.
every ancient thinker accepted the Stoic uses of sympatheia
critics rejected their defense of astrology and divination.

games.q: you're an emperor with a free minute. what exercise does Marcus give himself?
o: picture the universe as one living being.
games.why: he tells himself to regard the universe as one living being, all things woven into a single web.

practice: Choose one object near you, your shirt, a chair, the phone in your hand, and trace it backward one pair of hands at a time: who sewed it, grew it, mined it, packed it, drove it? You won't know their names; picture them anyway.
With each breath, add one more person to the web.

wordCard.voice: Sympatheia. Greek for being affected together: the Stoic idea that all things are connected, one woven whole.

orig.note: Greek: being affected together; the root of sympathy.

carryVoice: Your line: all woven. One living being, one web, with you somewhere in it. More tomorrow.
